vignette: Edward Thompson, a 68-year-old Republican state senator, has carried the weight of a night-time crash through more than a decade of public service. On a humid July evening in 2013, he was driving his campaign car from a rally to a town hall when a drunk driver from the interstate collided head-on. The impact ripped the windshield, splintered the front end, and left Edward clutching a splintered seat with blood seeping from his wrist. The acrid scent of spilled gasoline and the thud of metal against metal lodged in his memory as a single, vivid picture. In the days that followed, the mere smell of alcohol-whether in a bartender's glass or the scent of someone's breath-would trigger an immediate, involuntary discomfort, a sense of dread that compelled him to shun any drive, whether as a passenger or a driver. The image of cars smashed together, frozen in his mind as a snapshot, would burst into his thoughts whenever he passed a highway, and the physical pain he had felt in his chest during the collision would replay in his body as if the brakes had failed again. He blamed himself for the crash, telling himself that if he had been more careful, the accident might have been avoided. That character blame fed a hypervigilant need to guard against danger at all moments, and he felt as though anyone watching could see the terror etched into his face. The belief that the event was a direct consequence of his own failings made the quiet moments of his life feel suddenly sinister, as if silence itself was a threat waiting to erupt. The night after the crash, Edward woke repeatedly, listening for the faintest rumble that might indicate an approaching vehicle. The alarm of those midnight checks heightened his sense that danger could strike at any instant, even in the hush of a sleeping office. When the city's streets fell silent at dusk, he perceived a looming threat that pushed him to keep his phone on silent mode and to avoid any social gathering that might lead to a car ride. This constant state of alertness fed back into his memory: each restless night was punctuated by the sharp, physical recollection of his body clenching as the car slammed into the concrete. The pain, the suddenness, the way his fingers tingled in his pocket-each detail was replayed in his mind, and the images seemed to grow clearer the more he stared at them. His rumination over "what I should have done" tightened his self-blame, deepening the conviction that the accident was a verdict on his character. In turn, his relentless self-blame amplified his sense of threat, reinforcing the belief that the world was a hostile place that would judge him even from the corner of a passer-by's eye. The more he avoided driving, the more he sensed the smell of alcohol in a diner or a car wash as a trigger that forced him to stay out of vehicles altogether. Each avoidance act fed back into the cycle: the avoidance made him more alert to potential triggers, which made the avoidance feel even necessary. In therapy, Edward articulated how his self-blame rumination had become a self-fulfilling spiral. Every time he caught himself thinking "I was careless," a flash of the crash would flood his mind, bringing with it the throbbing pain in his shoulder and the image of the shattered windshield. Those memories, in turn, pushed him to check whether the brakes were still functioning before any car trip, even if it was just to the office. He avoided driving altogether, which left him stranded at his wife's house for weeks, missing briefings and public events. Each instance of avoidance, he noticed, intensified the feeling that he was being judged by strangers who could "see" the scar in his back, further feeding the threat perception that the world was a place of hidden dangers. The cycle became so entrenched that he feared stepping into a car would not only trigger his anxiety but might lead to another disaster. He had become convinced that the very act of driving could expose him to the same catastrophic event that had occurred a decade earlier. Now, years later, Edward sits on his office desk, staring at a photograph of his younger self beside a car wreck, feeling a mixture of relief and apprehension. The day he finally decided to seek help was when he realized that the constant state of hypervigilance was draining him, both physically and emotionally. He fears that continuing down this path will leave him isolated from his constituents and his family, yet he hopes that by addressing the painful memories and the self-blame that fuels his avoidance, he can reclaim the sense of safety that the accident took away. He is most afraid that the threat will never recede, and he is most hopeful that therapy might break the cycle that has defined his life since that night.
